title: A friend to myself
hookLine: Hecaton says: I have begun to be a friend to myself

lines: YOU IDIOT. WHY ARE YOU LIKE THIS.
cards: You idiot, you forgot again. Why are you like this. Plenty of inner voices talk like that.
Said out loud to a friend, those lines would cost the friendship. Inside a head, they can run for years.
In his sixth letter, Seneca passes along another line from Hecaton: the answer he gave when someone asked how far he'd come.

teach.b: Letter six opens with Seneca saying he feels himself not just improving but being transformed.

He adds, honestly, that he still has much to correct, and that this is itself a sign of progress: you can finally see faults you couldn't see before. Then he shares what pleased him in Hecaton that day.
Someone asks: what progress have you made? Hecaton answers, in Gummere's translation: I have begun to be a friend to myself. Not I've mastered my passions.
Not I've read everything. Just that.

teach.h: NEVER ALONE; A FRIEND TO ALL.
teach.b: Seneca calls this great progress, because such a person will never be alone. And someone who is a friend to himself, he adds, is a friend to everyone. The friendship starts at home and spreads outward.
What kind of friend? Not flattery, or excusing everything. A few days ago Seneca told Lucilius to choose friends carefully and then trust them wholly.
A good friend tells you the truth and stays on your side while doing it: honest about your faults, patient with them, never cruel.
Be to yourself what a true friend would be. And notice the word begun. Even Hecaton was only starting.

how: Some who practice Stoicism measure progress not by perfection but by how they treat themselves: honest about faults, patient with them, and on their own side.

o: a Greek god of friendship and loyalty
the friend Seneca wrote all his letters to
a Stoic whose progress was befriending himself

his answer was smaller: I have begun to be a friend to myself.

the friendship starts at home and spreads outward.
Seneca claims in letter six that he has nothing left to fix
he says he still has much to correct, and seeing it is progress.

games.q: you're Hecaton. someone asks: what progress have you made? what do you answer?
o: I've read every book in the school.
I have begun to be a friend to myself.
games.why: that's his answer, and Seneca calls it great progress: such a person is never alone, and is a friend to all.

practice: Think of something you've been hard on yourself about lately, and hear the voice you've been using. Now imagine a good friend heard all of it, and let them answer, something honest and something kind at once.
Then picture one small kindness for yourself, a glass of water, an early night, a real lunch, and let yourself be on your own side.

wordCard.voice: Hecaton, the Stoic Seneca quotes: his sign of progress was simply, I have begun to be a friend to myself. Today's word.
